text: Blisters: A blister is a small pocket of body fluid within the upper layers of the skin, usually caused by forceful rubbing (friction), burning, freezing, chemical exposure or infection. Most blisters are filled with a clear fluid, either serum or plasma.
Hair loss: Hair loss, also known as alopecia or baldness, refers to a loss of hair from part of the head or body. Typically at least the head is involved.

Itching: An itch is a sensation that causes a strong desire or reflex to scratch. Itches have many similarities to pain, and while both are unpleasant sensory experiences, their behavioral response patterns are different.

Leg ulcers: Venous ulcer is defined by the American Venous Forum as "a full-thickness defect of skin, most frequently in the ankle region, that fails to heal spontaneously and is sustained by chronic venous disease, based on venous duplex ultrasound testing." Venous ulcers are wounds that are thought to occur due to improper functioning of venous valves, usually of the legs. They are an important cause of chronic wounds, affecting 1% of the population.
Nail abnormalities: A presenting complaint characterised by nail abnormalities.
Photosensitivity: In medicine, photosensitivity is an abnormal reaction of the skin to light. There are two types: photoallergy and phototoxicity.

Rash: Skinheads Against Racial Prejudice (SHARP) are anti-racist skinheads who oppose white power skinheads, neo-fascists and racism within the skinhead community, particularly if they identify themselves as skinheads. SHARPs claim to reclaim the original multicultural identity of the original skinheads, hijacked by white power skinheads, who they sometimes deride as "boneheads".
Skin discoloration: Skin discoloration can be a side effect of certain medical therapies, for instance minocycline treatment and radiotherapy.

Skin lesions: A skin condition, also known as a cutaneous condition, is any medical condition that affects the integumentary system—the organ system that encloses the body and includes skin, nails, and related muscle and glands. The major function of this system is to act as a barrier against the external environment.
Skin lumps: A presenting complaint characterised by skin lumps.
Skin peeling: Desquamation, or peeling skin, is the shedding of dead cells from the outermost layer of skin.

Atopic dermatitis: Atopic dermatitis (AD), also known as atopic eczema, is chronic type of inflammation of the skin. Atopic dermatitis is also often called simply eczema, but "eczema" is also used to refer to dermatitis, the larger group of skin conditions. Common presenting complaints: Itching. Associated symptoms: none listed. Risk factors: none listed. Age relevance: . Sex relevance: . Acute or chronic: .

Bullous pemphigoid: Bullous pemphigoid is an autoimmune pruritic skin disease that typically occurs in people aged over 60, that may involve the formation of blisters (bullae) in the space between the epidermal and dermal skin layers. It is classified as a type II hypersensitivity reaction, which involves the formation of anti-hemidesmosome antibodies, causing a loss of keratinocytes to basement membrane adhesion. Common presenting complaints: Blisters. Associated symptoms: none listed. Risk factors: none listed. Age relevance: . Sex relevance: . Acute or chronic: .

Diabetic foot ulcer: Diabetic foot ulcer is a breakdown of the skin and sometimes deeper tissues of the foot that leads to sore formation. It is thought to occur due to abnormal pressure or mechanical stress chronically applied to the foot, usually with concomitant predisposing conditions such as peripheral sensory neuropathy, peripheral motor neuropathy, autonomic neuropathy or peripheral arterial disease. Common presenting complaints: Leg Ulcers. Associated symptoms: none listed. Risk factors: none listed. Age relevance: . Sex relevance: . Acute or chronic: .

Drug-induced photosensitivity: Light sensitivity or photosensitivity refers to a notable or increased reactivity to light. Apart from vision, human beings have many physiological and psychological responses to light. Common presenting complaints: Photosensitivity. Associated symptoms: Sunburn Like Reaction, Sun Exposed Area Rash. Risk factors: Photosensitizing Medication, Prolonged Sun Exposure. Age relevance: . Sex relevance: . Acute or chronic: .

Drug-induced photosensitivity red flags. Red flag (RF_SEVERE_PHOTOSENSITIVITY_REACTION) triggered by symptom 'SUNBURN_LIKE_REACTION': Widespread blistering or skin peeling after sun exposure on a new medication.

Drug rash with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms syndrome: In medicine, a drug eruption is an adverse drug reaction of the skin. Most drug-induced cutaneous reactions are mild and disappear when the offending drug is withdrawn. Common presenting complaints: Rash. Associated symptoms: Fever, Widespread Rash, Facial Edema, Lymphadenopathy. Risk factors: New Medication Exposure, Immunocompromised. Age relevance: all_ages. Sex relevance: all_sexes. Acute or chronic: acute_subacute.

Drug rash with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms syndrome red flags. Red flag (RF_BREATHING) triggered by symptom 'DIFFICULTY_BREATHING': present. Red flag (RF_JAUNDICE) triggered by symptom 'JAUNDICE': present. Red flag (RF_RAPID_SYSTEMIC_DETERIORATION) triggered by symptom 'SYSTEMIC_ILLNESS': present. Red flag (RF_DRESS_ORGAN_INVOLVEMENT) triggered by symptom 'FACIAL_EDEMA': Facial swelling with fever and widespread rash after a new medication — possible systemic organ involvement, treat as emergency.

Drug rash with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms syndrome differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Unspecified Viral Infection Characterized By Skin And Mucous Membrane Lesions: Both can present with fever and rash; recent drug exposure plus eosinophilia/systemic organ involvement favors DRESS. Compared to Other Specified Viral Infections Characterized By Skin And Mucous Membrane Lesions: Viral exanthem can mimic drug eruption; medication timeline and systemic features help distinguish.

Epidermoid cyst: An epidermoid cyst or epidermal inclusion cyst is a benign cyst usually found on the skin. The cyst develops out of ectodermal tissue. Common presenting complaints: Skin Lumps. Associated symptoms: none listed. Risk factors: none listed. Age relevance: . Sex relevance: . Acute or chronic: .

Exfoliative dermatitis: Erythroderma is an inflammatory skin disease with redness and scaling that affects nearly the entire cutaneous surface. This term applies when 90% or more of the skin is affected. Common presenting complaints: Skin Peeling. Associated symptoms: none listed. Risk factors: none listed. Age relevance: . Sex relevance: . Acute or chronic: .

Herpes zoster: Shingles, also known as herpes zoster or zona, is a viral disease characterized by a painful skin rash with blisters in a localized area. Typically the rash occurs in a single, wide mark either on the left or right side of the body or face. Common presenting complaints: Blisters. Associated symptoms: Dermatomal Vesicular Rash, Burning Tingling Pain, Fever. Risk factors: Age Over 50, Immunocompromised, Prior Varicella Infection. Age relevance: . Sex relevance: . Acute or chronic: .

Herpes zoster red flags. Red flag (RF_ZOSTER_OPHTHALMIC) triggered by symptom 'DERMATOMAL_VESICULAR_RASH': Rash involves the eye, eyelid, or tip of the nose — risk of vision loss, needs same-day ophthalmology/medical review.

Lipoma: A lipoma is a benign tumor made of fat tissue. They are generally soft to the touch, movable, and painless. Common presenting complaints: Skin Lumps. Associated symptoms: Soft Mobile Skin Lump, Slow Growing Painless Mass. Risk factors: Family History Lipoma, Obesity. Age relevance: . Sex relevance: . Acute or chronic: .

Lipoma red flags. Red flag (RF_RAPID_LUMP_CHANGE) triggered by symptom 'SOFT_MOBILE_SKIN_LUMP': Lump has grown quickly, become hard/fixed to underlying tissue, or painful — refer to rule out liposarcoma.

Melasma: Melasma is a common skin disorder characterized by tan, brown, or grayish hyperpigmented patches, usually on the face. Common presenting complaints: Skin Discoloration. Associated symptoms: none listed. Risk factors: none listed. Age relevance: . Sex relevance: . Acute or chronic: .

Nail psoriasis: Psoriatic onychodystrophy is a nail disease which is common in those with psoriasis, with reported incidences varying from 10% to 78%. Elderly patients and those with psoriatic arthritis are more likely to have psoriatic nails. Common presenting complaints: Nail Abnormalities. Associated symptoms: none listed. Risk factors: none listed. Age relevance: . Sex relevance: . Acute or chronic: .

Nonscarring hair loss, unspecified: Non scarring hair loss, also known as noncicatricial alopecia, is the loss of hair without any scarring being present. There is typically little inflammation and irritation, but hair loss is significant. Common presenting complaints: Hair Loss. Associated symptoms: Diffuse Hair Thinning, Increased Hair Shedding, Scalp Itching. Risk factors: Recent Illness Or Stress, Thyroid Disorder, Iron Deficiency, Family History Hair Loss. Age relevance: all_ages. Sex relevance: all_sexes. Acute or chronic: variable.

Nonscarring hair loss, unspecified red flags. Red flag (RF_SUDDEN_PATCHY_HAIR_LOSS) triggered by symptom 'SCALP_ITCHING': Sudden patchy (not diffuse) hair loss with scalp redness or scarring — refer to dermatologist to rule out scarring alopecia.

Nonscarring hair loss, unspecified differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Other Specified Nonscarring Hair Loss: Both are nonscarring hair-loss categories; the specified category should be used when the cause/pattern is documented.

Onychomycosis: Onychomycosis, also known as tinea unguium, is a fungal infection of the nail. Symptoms may include white or yellow nail discoloration, thickening of the nail, and separation of the nail from the nail bed. Common presenting complaints: Nail Abnormalities. Associated symptoms: Nail Thickening, Nail Discoloration, Brittle Crumbly Nail. Risk factors: Diabetes, Nail Trauma, Communal Shower Exposure. Age relevance: . Sex relevance: . Acute or chronic: .

Onychomycosis red flags. Red flag (RF_NAIL_SECONDARY_INFECTION) triggered by symptom 'NAIL_THICKENING': Spreading redness, swelling, warmth, or pus around the nail — possible secondary bacterial infection.

Other early skin lesions of yaws: Yaws is a tropical infection of the skin, bones, and joints caused by the spirochete bacterium Treponema pallidum pertenue. The disease begins with a round, hard swelling of the skin, 2 to 5 cm in diameter. Common presenting complaints: Skin Lesions. Associated symptoms: Hard Swelling Of The Skin, Ulcer, Joint And Bone Pain. Risk factors: Treponema Pallidum Pertenue Spread By Direct Contact. Age relevance: all_ages. Sex relevance: all_sexes. Acute or chronic: subacute.

Other specified nonscarring hair loss: Non scarring hair loss, also known as noncicatricial alopecia, is the loss of hair without any scarring being present. There is typically little inflammation and irritation, but hair loss is significant. Common presenting complaints: Hair Loss. Associated symptoms: none listed. Risk factors: none listed. Age relevance: all_ages. Sex relevance: all_sexes. Acute or chronic: variable.

Other specified nonscarring hair loss differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Nonscarring Hair Loss Unspecified: Unspecified nonscarring hair loss remains a fallback when the documented cause/pattern cannot be specified.

Other specified viral infections characterized by skin and mucous membrane lesions: A viral infection presenting with characteristic skin and mucous membrane lesions, not otherwise specified. Common presenting complaints: Skin Lesions. Associated symptoms: none listed. Risk factors: none listed. Age relevance: all_ages. Sex relevance: all_sexes. Acute or chronic: acute.

Polymorphic light eruption: Polymorphous light eruption (PLE) is a non-life-threatening and potentially distressing skin condition that presents with itchy red small bumps on sun-exposed skin, particularly the face, neck, forearms and legs. It generally appears 30 minutes to a few hours after sun exposure and may last between one and 14 days. Common presenting complaints: Photosensitivity. Associated symptoms: none listed. Risk factors: none listed. Age relevance: . Sex relevance: . Acute or chronic: .

Psoriasis vulgaris: Psoriasis is a long-lasting, noncontagious autoimmune disease characterized by patches of abnormal skin. These areas are red, pink, or purple, dry, itchy, and scaly. Common presenting complaints: Skin Peeling. Associated symptoms: none listed. Risk factors: none listed. Age relevance: . Sex relevance: . Acute or chronic: .

Scabies: Scabies is a contagious human skin infestation by the tiny (0.2–0.45 mm) mite Sarcoptes scabiei, variety hominis. The word is from Latin: scabere, lit. 'to scratch'. Common presenting complaints: Itching. Associated symptoms: none listed. Risk factors: none listed. Age relevance: . Sex relevance: . Acute or chronic: .

Unspecified viral infection characterized by skin and mucous membrane lesions: An acute viral infection presenting with diffuse skin eruptions and mucous membrane ulcerations of uncertain etiology. Common presenting complaints: Skin Lesions. Associated symptoms: Difficulty Breathing, Coughing Up Mucus, Poor Growth, Fatty Stool. Risk factors: Genetic (autosomal Recessive). Age relevance: all_ages. Sex relevance: all_sexes. Acute or chronic: acute.
Unspecified viral infection characterized by skin and mucous membrane lesions red flags. Red flag (RF_BREATHING) triggered by symptom 'DIFFICULTY_BREATHING': present.

Unspecified viral infection characterized by skin and mucous membrane lesions differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Other Specified Viral Infections Characterized By Skin And Mucous Membrane Lesions: The distinction is mainly whether the viral cause/clinical syndrome is specified.

Venous ulcers are wounds that are thought to occur due to improper functioning of venous valves, usually of the legs. They are an important cause of chronic wounds, affecting 1% of the population. Vitiligo: Vitiligo is a chronic autoimmune disorder that causes skin to lose pigment in patches that vary in size and can appear anywhere on the body. Common presenting complaints: Skin Discoloration. Associated symptoms: none listed. Risk factors: none listed. Age relevance: . Sex relevance: . Acute or chronic: .
